item.title: Osaka Sake & Izakaya Tasting: A Night of Drinking Osaka — Guide
item.description: Osaka takes drinking as seriously as eating, and a night in its izakaya and sake bars is one of the warmest experiences the city offers. The options run from tachinomi standing bars crammed under railway arches around Umeda and Namba, where a few hundred yen buys a glass and a skewer, to specialist sake bars pouring flights from breweries across the Kansai region and English-friendly guided tastings that walk you through junmai, ginjo and the differences between them.

item.title: Pontocho: Kyoto's Atmospheric Dining Alley — Guide
item.description: Pontocho is a single narrow lane, running for several hundred metres between Shijo and Sanjo alongside the Kamo River, and it is the most atmospheric place to eat and drink in Kyoto. Barely two metres wide and closed to cars, it is lined on both sides with wooden machiya houses turned into restaurants and bars, hung with lanterns and the crest of the district, a stylised plover. The range runs from exclusive kaiseki restaurants with summer platforms out over the river to tiny standing bars and yakitori counters.

item.title: Kokubuncho: Sendai's Neon-Lit Nightlife District — Guide
item.description: Kokubuncho is Tohoku’s largest entertainment district, a dense grid of neon-lit streets packed with izakaya (Japanese gastropubs), bars, karaoke boxes and restaurants a short walk from Sendai Station. By day it looks like an ordinary commercial street; by night, thousands of illuminated signs turn it into one of northern Japan’s liveliest nightlife scenes, popular with both locals winding down after work and visitors seeking a lively evening out. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Aoba-ku, Sendai, Miyagi Hours Evening onward, busiest after 19:00 Admission Free to walk; drinks/food extra Time needed 2+ hours Best time Friday and Saturday nights What to See A dense grid of neon-lit izakaya, bars and karaoke boxes.

item.title: Dotonbori Guide: Neon, Street Food & the Glico Sign
item.description: No place sums up Osaka’s “eat till you drop” spirit like Dotonbori — a canal lined with giant animated billboards, a forest of neon, mechanical crabs and dragons crawling across shopfronts, and the legendary Glico running man glowing over the water. This is the city’s most famous entertainment and street-food strip, packed with restaurants, izakaya, and food stalls, and at night it becomes a riot of light and crowds. It’s loud, brash, delicious, and unmistakably Osaka.

item.title: Dotonbori Halloween Guide: What It's Really Like in Osaka
item.description: Around October 31, costumed crowds gather in and around Dotonbori for an informal Halloween street party — Osaka’s equivalent of Tokyo’s Shibuya scramble. It’s spontaneous and unofficial: there’s no organised event, no stage, no tickets — just thousands of people in costume filling the Ebisubashi bridge and Dotonbori canalside to see and be seen. It can be fun and photogenic, but it’s also extremely crowded and increasingly managed by police. Here’s an honest picture of what it’s actually like and how to do it sensibly — plus better alternatives.

item.title: Kokusai-dori Guide: Shopping, Eats & Access (Naha)
item.description: Kokusai-dori (“International Street”) is Naha’s bustling main thoroughfare — a roughly 1.6 km stretch lined with souvenir shops, restaurants, izakaya, cafés and street performers. Rebuilt in the years after WWII and nicknamed the “Miracle Mile,” it’s the liveliest place in Okinawa to shop for local crafts and snacks, sample Okinawan cuisine, and feel the island’s easygoing energy. Dip into the covered market arcades just off the main drag for a more local, atmospheric experience.

item.title: Namba & Shinsaibashi Guide: Osaka's Shopping & Nightlife Heart
item.description: If Umeda is Osaka’s polished northern hub, Namba and Shinsaibashi are the buzzing southern heart — Minami — where the city shops, eats, and plays late into the night. A continuous web of covered arcades, brand boutiques, depachika food halls, vintage and youth-fashion streets, and the neon of Dotonbori all link together here in a walkable, endlessly energetic sprawl. Whether you want luxury labels, cheap fashion, electronics, or just to ride the wave of the crowd, this is where Osaka’s pulse beats hardest.

item.title: Sapporo Guide: Odori Park, Susukino & Things to Do
item.description: Sapporo, Hokkaido’s vibrant capital and Japan’s fifth-largest city, is the gateway to the north and a destination in its own right. Laid out on an easy American-style grid, it centres on the long green ribbon of Odori Park, runs north to the historic Clock Tower and former government buildings, and south into the neon buzz of Susukino, one of Japan’s great nightlife and dining districts. Add legendary food — miso ramen, soup curry, jingisukan and crab — plus year-round festivals, and Sapporo is the perfect base for exploring Hokkaido.

item.title: Shibuya Halloween: What's Really Happening Now (Honest Guide)
item.description: For years, Shibuya’s Halloween was famous as one of the world’s largest spontaneous costume gatherings — tens of thousands of revellers in elaborate outfits flooding the scramble crossing with no organiser, no tickets, just an enormous self-generating street party. If you’ve read older travel guides, that’s the image they sell. Here’s the honest, current reality: Shibuya no longer wants this, and is actively asking people — especially crowds and tourists — to stay away on Halloween.

item.title: Tokyo Leisure & Entertainment Guide
item.description: Tokyo offers more ways to spend an evening — or an entire week — than almost any city on earth. From sumo tournaments and kabuki theatre to vinyl record hunting and 3am karaoke, this guide covers the best leisure experiences in the city. 🎨 Digital Art & Immersive Experiences teamLab Planets — Toyosu Access: Shin-Toyosu Station (Yurikamome Line) — 5 min walk Hours: 9:00–21:00 (varies seasonally) Entry: ¥3,200 (advance booking required)
